nota_resistencia: Simple average of the published tests we found (Mikel, 2026-11-20: «when you find two or three references, put the average and that's it»). It varies a lot with the condition of the line and how the knot is tied.

fichas.para: Tie the line to a hook, a lure or a swivel.
fichas.resumen: One of the easiest and most reliable hook knots. It works especially well with braid, which tends to slip in other knots.
pasos: Double about 15 cm of the end of the line and pass the doubled line through the hook eye.
With the doubled line, tie a loose overhand knot, leaving the hook hanging from the loop.
Pass the whole hook through the loop that is left.
Wet the knot and pull the main line and the tag end at the same time until it seats on the eye.
Trim the tag end, leaving a few millimetres.
fichas.ojo: The hook or lure has to pass through the loop: with big lures or treble hooks you need a long loop and it is awkward.

fichas.para: Tie the line to a hook, a lure or a swivel.
fichas.resumen: The classic hook knot for thin and medium nylon. Quick to tie without looking.
pasos: Pass the end of the line through the hook eye.
Make five or more turns with the tag end around the main line.
Pass the tag end through the small loop left next to the eye.
Then pass it through the big loop that has just formed.
Wet it and tighten by pulling the main line; trim the tag end.
fichas.ojo: Not recommended with thick lines (over about 30 lb breaking strain): it is hard to tighten properly. With thick line four turns may be enough.

fichas.para: Tie to hooks and swivels, make loops and, doubled (one on each line), join two lines.
fichas.resumen: A knot for almost everything: you can tie on the hook, make a sliding loop or, by tying one on each end, join two lines (the «double uni»). It works with braid and with nylon.
pasos: Pass the tag end through the eye and bring it back parallel to the main line, forming a loop.
Make four to six turns with the tag end around both lines, inside the loop.
Wet it and pull the tag end to close the turns.
Slide the knot down to the eye by pulling the main line; trim the tag end.
To join two lines (double uni): overlap the ends, tie a uni with each one around the other and pull both lines so they come together.
fichas.ojo: As a line-to-line join it is somewhat weaker than the same knot tied to a large eye; to join braid to a fluorocarbon leader, the FG is slimmer and passes better through the guides.

fichas.para: Join the braid main line to a fluorocarbon or nylon leader.
fichas.resumen: The most used braid-to-leader join in spinning and jigging: very slim and strong, and it passes through the guides without catching when casting.
pasos: Keep the braid tight (for example, held in your mouth or on the rod with the drag locked).
Cross the leader over the braid and wrap the braid around the leader, alternating over and under, about twenty times.
Without releasing the tension, finish with several half hitches of the braid around the leader.
Wet it and tighten hard by pulling both lines; trim the leader tag end.
Finish with a few half hitches of the braid on itself and trim.
fichas.ojo: It is hard to learn: the details matter and you have to keep the braid tight the whole time. Better to practise it at home before going out.

fichas.para: Join lines of different type or thickness: nylon to braid, or braid to wire.
fichas.resumen: A simpler alternative to the FG for joining two different lines.
pasos: Double the end of the thicker line to form a loop.
Pass the thinner line through the loop.
Wrap it ten or twelve turns around both legs of the loop, working towards the tip.
Bring the tag end out through the loop, on the same side it went in.
Wet it, tighten by pulling both lines and trim the tag ends.
fichas.ojo: Only moderately easy to tie; the turns must sit neatly, without riding over each other.

fichas.para: Make a small loop at the end of the leader, to change leaders loop to loop.
fichas.resumen: A small loop that sits in line with the line: used to attach and change leaders or rigs without cutting.
pasos: Make a first loop with the tag end, passing it behind the main line.
Make a second loop in front of the first.
Pass the tag end between the two loops.
Push the second loop through the first.
Tighten by pulling the second loop and the main line; trim the tag end.
fichas.ojo: It is easier to tie in the hand than with the hook already on.

fichas.para: Tie the leader directly to the hook shank, for natural bait.
fichas.resumen: The line comes out in line with the hook shank, which helps the hook set. It was created for spade-end hooks (no eye) and is still widely used with bait.
pasos: Pass the end of the leader through the eye (or lay it against the spade), leaving a good length of tag along the shank.
Form a loop along the shank.
Make five to seven tight turns around the shank and the line, from the eye towards the bend.
Hold the turns and pull the main line to close them.
Tighten by pulling the line and the tag end; trim the tag end.
fichas.ojo: The turns must sit together on the shank, without crossing.

fichas.para: Tie the line to a hook or lure.
fichas.resumen: A hook knot that keeps the line's strength very well. It works with nylon, braid and fluorocarbon.
pasos: Pass the tag end through the eye and leave plenty of tag.
Wrap the tag end around both lines (the main line and the tag itself) towards the eye.
Pass the tag end through the first loop, next to the eye.
Then pass it through the loop that has just formed at the top.
Wet it and tighten by pulling the main line; trim the tag end.
fichas.ojo: The thicker the line, the fewer the turns: about seven or eight with thin line and about three with thick line. Do not let the turns ride over each other.

fichas.para: Make a loop in the middle of the line, standing out at a right angle, to hang an extra hook (paternoster, bottom rigs).
fichas.resumen: The basis of multi-hook rigs: each loop stands off the line and the hook does not tangle with the main line.
pasos: Make a big loop at the point on the line where you want the dropper.
Wrap one side of the loop over the other several times (five to seven), leaving a gap in the centre.
Push the centre of the big loop through that gap.
Hold the loop that comes out and pull both ends of the line to close it.
Adjust the size of the loop before fully tightening.
fichas.ojo: The loop should not be very long: it tangles and twists more. With nylon, the knot changes shape as you tighten it; that is normal.

fichas.para: The traditional line: a single filament of polyamide.
fichas.resumen: Cheap, easy to knot and stretchy. It is the most versatile and the one almost everyone starts with.
como_es: It stretches quite a lot: it cushions the fish's head shakes and forgives mistakes on the strike, but transmits bites less well.
It almost floats (density close to that of water): it stays on the surface or sinks very slowly.
It absorbs some water and sunlight degrades it: over time it loses strength. It is worth changing it every season.
It has memory: if it stays on the spool for a long time it comes off in coils.
It resists abrasion reasonably well, but less than fluorocarbon of the same diameter.

colores.para: The most discreet in clear water.
Blends with the bottom and the water; discreet and a little easier for the angler to see.
Easy to see from above the water to follow the line and spot bites, but the fish sees it more too: best with a clear leader.

usos_costa: Main line for surfcasting and bottom fishing from the beach.
Float fishing: it floats and helps keep the float in place.
General-purpose leaders when the water is somewhat coloured.
Shock leaders and tapered lines for powerful casts.
usos_embarcacion: Cheap main line for bait fishing at anchor and on the drift.
Surface trolling, where the stretch cushions sudden runs.
General-purpose leaders.
fichas.ojo: Check it every trip: if the line feels rough or fuzzy when you run your fingers along it, cut that section off. Sun and salt age it even when it is not used.

fichas.para: An improved nylon: a blend of two or more types of nylon in a single filament.
fichas.resumen: It handles like nylon but stretches less and resists abrasion better. It costs a bit more.
como_es: It stretches less than normal nylon: a bit more sensitivity without losing the cushioning.
Better resistance to abrasion and sudden jerks than a nylon of the same diameter.
It is just as easy to knot as nylon.
It floats or sinks slowly, like nylon.

colores.para: Discreet in clear water.
Discreet and a little more visible to the angler.
To follow the line; a clear leader is advisable.

usos_costa: Main line for light spinning and float fishing when you want a bit more sensitivity than with nylon.
Leaders and shock leaders on rocky ground.
usos_embarcacion: Main line for fishing at anchor and on the drift over hard ground.
General-purpose leaders.
fichas.ojo: It is more expensive than nylon and, like nylon, it degrades in the sun: store it in the shade.

fichas.para: A fluoropolymer (PVDF) filament designed mainly for leaders.
fichas.resumen: It is the line that is least visible underwater, it sinks and it stands up very well to abrasion from rocks and shells. Its natural place is the leader.
como_es: It bends light almost like water does (refractive index ~1.42 compared with 1.33 for water and ~1.5–1.6 for nylon): that is why it is less visible. It helps, but it does not make it invisible.
It sinks (it is quite a lot denser than water): it takes the bait and the leader down towards the bottom.
It is the most abrasion-resistant for the same diameter.
It does not absorb water and stands up well to the sun: it lasts longer than nylon.
It is stiffer and harder to knot: always wet the knot before tightening.

colores.para: It is almost always used like this: it is what people buying fluorocarbon are after.
Some brands tint it for particular bottoms or waters; the advantage is debated.

usos_costa: Leaders for bass, white seabream, gilthead bream and other wary fish in clear water.
Leaders on rock, mussel beds or shells, where nylon gets cut.
Shock leader in surfcasting over hard ground.
usos_embarcacion: Leaders for jigging, spinning and fishing at anchor in clear water.
Leaders for wary species and for fishing over rock.
Heavy leaders against teeth that are not very sharp when you do not want to use wire.
fichas.ojo: As a main line on the reel it is heavy, sinks and has memory: it is almost always used only as a leader. It is expensive; buy leader spools, not main-line spools.

fichas.para: Several polyethylene fibres braided (4, 8 or more) into a single line.
fichas.resumen: Very thin and very strong for its diameter, it hardly stretches: you feel everything. It needs a nylon or fluorocarbon leader.
como_es: It hardly stretches: it transmits bites and the bottom instantly and sets the hook better at distance.
Much thinner than a nylon of the same strength: it casts further and wind and current drag it less.
It floats.
It is rated by PE number (higher means thicker) as well as by kilos.
X4 (4 fibres): rougher but more abrasion-resistant. X8 (8 fibres): rounder and smoother, casts further but frays sooner on rock.
The sun does not affect it the way it affects nylon, but it frays with sideways abrasion.

colores.para: Discreet: the most used in spinning.
Visible from far away: to follow the line, see bites on the line and cast at night with a torch.
To know how much line has gone out: each colour is 10 m. Some also have a mark every metre. Designed for vertical fishing.

usos_costa: Spinning with lures: the main line is almost always braid.
Long-distance surfcasting, with a nylon or fluorocarbon shock leader.
Bottom fishing where feeling the bite matters.
usos_embarcacion: Jigging and slow jigging, with multicolour braid to know the depth.
Vertical bottom fishing and drifting in deep water: thin line bows less in the current.
Spinning and popping from the boat.
fichas.ojo: Always with a leader: it is very visible and sideways abrasion against rocks cuts it. Do not tie braid with nylon knots (it slips): use a palomar or FG. It cuts your fingers if you grab it while a fish is pulling.

fichas.para: Steel wire leaders, single-strand or braided, sometimes nylon-coated.
fichas.resumen: For toothy fish that cut through any line: conger eel, bluefish, barracuda, sea pike or shark.
como_es: No toothy fish can cut it.
It is stiff and visible: some fish get wary and the lure loses some of its action.
Coated braided wire is more flexible; single-strand wire is stiffer and thinner.
It kinks and frays: check it after every fish.

colores.para: The classic; it shines underwater.
More discreet; the one recommended in clear water.

usos_costa: Bottom fishing for conger eel from rocks, harbours and breakwaters: wire leader, or very heavy nylon if you prefer the fish not to notice it so much.
Spinning and bottom fishing when bluefish or other toothy fish come in.
A short length (about 15–30 cm) in front of the lure or hook.
usos_embarcacion: Conger eel over rock and wrecks, with a wire or very heavy nylon leader.
Trolling and spinning for toothy predators (barracuda, sea pike, shark).
Short leaders above the lure, joined with a swivel or snap.
fichas.ojo: Use it only when there are teeth: otherwise it scares fish and costs you bites. For conger, many anglers use very heavy nylon (130 lb and up) instead of wire: they cannot cut wire, but if the fish swallows the hook wire does it more harm; with nylon, check for abrasion after every fish.

fichas.para: A braid with a lead core inside that makes the line sink on its own.
fichas.resumen: For trolling in mid-water or near the bottom without using leads or diving planers.
como_es: It changes colour every 10 yards (about 9 m): you count how many colours are out.
Rule of thumb: each colour goes down about 1.5 m at slow trolling speed (about 4 km/h); it changes a lot with speed and lure.
It is thick and very visible: it needs a long nylon or fluorocarbon leader.

colores.para: To work out the depth the lure is running at.

usos_costa: Not used from the shore.
usos_embarcacion: Bottom and mid-water trolling from a boat.
Always with a long leader (several metres) of nylon or fluorocarbon.
fichas.ojo: The colours are a guide, not a measurement: with current or more speed the lure rises. Check on the echo sounder whether you are touching the bottom.

Bass Pro: lead core guide

fichas.para: Which line colour to use depending on the water and what you want to see yourself.
fichas.resumen: Colour is a balance between you seeing the line and the fish not seeing it. The usual solution: a visible main line and a clear leader.
como_es: The fish mainly sees the part close to the bait: that is why the leader matters more than the main line.
In clear water, clear fluorocarbon is the least visible.
In coloured water or at night, colour matters much less.
The idea that red disappears underwater is debated: some divers say it looks black.

colores.para: Leaders in clear water and for wary fish.
Discreet main line for clear water.
Main line to see bites and follow the line; always with a clear leader.
Knowing how much line has gone out (vertical fishing and trolling).

usos_costa: Surfcasting: visible-coloured main line to see the line and a clear leader.
Spinning in clear water: green or grey braid with a fluorocarbon leader.
usos_embarcacion: Jigging: multicolour braid with a fluorocarbon leader.
Trolling: the long clear leader is what the fish sees.
fichas.ojo: There are no conclusive studies on which colour each species sees: take this as a practical guide, not a rule.

fichas.para: The hooks are on short snoods above the lead, which sits at the very bottom.
fichas.resumen: The most used bottom rig: it carries several baits at once and keeps them off the bottom.
como_es: The lead goes at the end; the snoods come off the rig body with swivels, beads or knots.
It carries one, two or three hooks: more baits, more scent in the water.
When it bites, the fish feels the weight of the lead and often hooks itself.
Sliding variant (running paternoster): the rig body runs on the main line and the fish feels less.
medidas: Two-hook surfcasting rigs are usually about 170–180 cm in total, with snoods of about 70 cm.
Short snoods tangle less when casting; long ones move the bait more in the current.
Snoods a little thinner than the rig body: if you snag, only one breaks.
usos_costa: Beach surfcasting: the beach rig par excellence.
Clean or mixed ground for white seabream, gilthead bream, sand steenbras, flatfish and similar.
On very rocky ground, better with a weak link for the lead (so the lead breaks off and not the whole rig).
usos_embarcacion: At anchor and on the drift: several hooks at different heights off the bottom.
Mixed bottom fishing (red seabream, pandora, horse mackerel…).
fichas.ojo: With strong wind and long casts, long snoods tangle: use bait clips to hold them during the cast.

fichas.para: The lead runs freely on the main line, above a swivel; below it goes the hook length.
fichas.resumen: The fish takes the bait and swims off without feeling the weight of the lead: for big, wary fish.
como_es: A running lead (or a clip with a lead) runs on the main line; a bead protects the knot at the swivel.
The hook length comes off the swivel, usually with a single hook.
Positive bite: the line runs through the lead and shows on the rod tip.
medidas: A hook length of 1 to 1.5 m to start with on the beach.
More current, longer hook length: the bait moves more naturally.
Just enough lead to hold the bottom in whatever current there is.
usos_costa: Bass, gilthead bream and big fish from the beach or rocks.
Night bottom fishing with big baits.
Conger eel from harbours or rocks (with a cut-resistant leader).
usos_embarcacion: At anchor in deep water for big bottom fish (conger eel, pollack, rays).
Slow drifting with a single big bait.
fichas.ojo: If the lead is too light, the current drags it and the hook length wraps around the main line: go up in lead before lengthening the hook length.

fichas.para: A rig in which the lead and the hook travel together on the cast and, when the fish bites, the lead rises above it.
fichas.resumen: It casts far and protects the bait during the cast; when the hook is set, the lead moves away from the fish and snags less on rock.
como_es: The rig body runs through a swivel (the «pulley») attached to the main line.
On the cast, the hook is held against the lead with a clip: more distance and the bait does not break up.
While playing the fish, the lead stays above and rises over the rocks.
medidas: Around one rod length in total; the hook length, from 60 cm to 1 m.
Heavy rig body (abrasion-resistant) and a slightly thinner snood.
usos_costa: Long-distance surfcasting on clean beaches.
Ground with rock or weed for big fish: the lead snags less on the retrieve.
usos_embarcacion: Rarely used from a boat: when fishing vertically it is not needed.
fichas.ojo: The rig works doubled over: check the rig body for wear at the swivel every few fish.

fichas.para: The bait hangs from a float at the depth you choose; a stop knot on the main line sets how far it goes down.
fichas.resumen: For fishing in mid-water or close to the rocks without snagging: white seabream, bass, mullet, ballan wrasse, mackerel…
como_es: Fixed float for shallow water (up to 1.5–2 m) or a sliding float with stop knot and bead for deeper water.
Shot under the float until only the tip shows: that way you notice even the most delicate bite.
The final hook length is usually thinner than the main line.
medidas: Depth: start at one metre and go deeper until they bite; for ballan wrasse, the bait should brush the bottom.
A bigger float the rougher the sea and the deeper the water.
Final hook length of 50 cm to 1 m.
usos_costa: Breakwaters, harbours and rocks: in mid-water next to the weed.
Mullet and other species in calm water, with a small float.
Bass with live bait under the float.
usos_embarcacion: At anchor or on a slow drift next to the rocks, with a float.
Mackerel and horse mackerel in mid-water.
fichas.ojo: The tide changes the depth: readjust the stop knot regularly.

fichas.para: A lead on the main line, a swivel that stops it and a leader with a hook behind.
fichas.resumen: The lead drags along the bottom and the bait or soft plastic floats a little above it: very good for bottom fish that look upwards.
como_es: Bullet or barrel lead running on the main line, a bead and the swivel.
Leader with one hook; natural bait or soft plastic.
Cast it and retrieve very slowly, dragging the lead.
medidas: Short leader (about 15–30 cm in the guides consulted) to keep the bait close to the bottom; longer so it moves more.
Lead according to depth and current.
usos_costa: Flatfish (sole, turbot) and other bottom fish on sand, with a slow retrieve.
Soft plastic fishing from the beach and from rocks with clean ground.
usos_embarcacion: Slow drifting over sand for flatfish.
fichas.ojo: On rock it snags a lot: it is a clean-ground rig.

fichas.para: A rig with many small hooks dressed with feathers or flash; the lead goes at the bottom.
fichas.resumen: Used to catch live bait (mackerel, horse mackerel, sardine, bogue…) when there are shoals.
como_es: 6 to 10 small hooks on short snoods.
It needs no bait: the flash is enough; some anglers add a small piece.
Lower it to the shoal and lift and drop it gently.
medidas: Just enough lead for it to drop slowly through the shoal: with too much lead it goes through the shoal too fast.
More lead if it tangles: the rig stays tighter.
usos_costa: Harbours and breakwaters when mackerel or horse mackerel come in.
To get live bait for bass or squid.
usos_embarcacion: Over shoals marked on the echo sounder.
Before going out to fish with live bait.
fichas.ojo: Lots of hooks together: it tangles and pricks. Unhook with pliers and keep it on its winder. Respect minimum sizes with bait fish too.

fichas.para: A length of fluorocarbon or nylon between the braid and the lure.
fichas.resumen: It protects against abrasion, hides the braid and adds cushioning: braid never goes straight to the lure.
como_es: It is joined to the braid with a slim knot (FG or Albright) and to the lure with a knot or a snap.
Fluorocarbon in clear water or around rock; nylon if you want more stretch.
If there are teeth, a short length of wire at the end.
medidas: Length: the knot with the braid should not go into the guides when casting (or it should pass through them as a very slim knot).
Clear water, longer leader; coloured water, it can be shorter.
Thickness: a leader stronger than the braid is pointless; around rock, a little thicker.
usos_costa: Spinning for bass, bluefish and other predators from the shore.
Fishing with soft plastics and stickbaits on rock: the leader is what rubs.
usos_embarcacion: Spinning and jigging from the boat.
Popping for tuna and big predators with a heavy leader.
fichas.ojo: Check the last few centimetres after every fish or snag: the leader gets nicked and it is the first thing to break.

fichas.nombre: Leader thickness and length: how to choose
fichas.para: Practical rules for choosing leader diameter and length depending on the water, the bottom and the fish.
fichas.resumen: The leader is what the fish sees and what rubs: thinner gets more bites, thicker holds more. You look for the balance.
como_es: Thinner than the main line (or snoods thinner than the rig body): if something breaks, let it be only the leader.
Fluorocarbon is slightly thinner than nylon of the same strength.
With rock, shells or fish with hard scales or spines, thicker.
More current, longer leader so the bait moves naturally.
medidas: Beach surfcasting: final fluorocarbon hook lengths of 0.30–0.35 mm are common for medium-sized fish.
Clear water and wary fish: thinner, longer leader.
Coloured water or at night: you can go thicker without losing bites.
usos_costa: Clean beach: thin leader.
Rock and mussels: thick leader or fluorocarbon.
Toothy fish: wire or very heavy nylon.
usos_embarcacion: Rocky bottom: thick snoods.
Very clear water in summer: thin and long.
fichas.ojo: These are guides, not rules: the condition of the line and the knot matter more than the exact diameter.

fichas.nombre: Hook sizes: how they are numbered
fichas.para: How to read a hook number and why a size 2 is not the same in every brand.
fichas.resumen: Up to size 1, the higher the number, the smaller the hook. After that come the «aughts» (1/0, 2/0…), where the higher the number, the bigger the hook. And almost all of us fish with hooks that are too big.
como_es: Order from small to large: … 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 1, 1/0, 2/0, 3/0, 4/0…
1/0 comes after 1; 4/0 is quite a lot bigger than 1/0.
Wire thickness is marked with «X»: a 2X is thicker and stronger than the standard hook of its size.
There is no standard between brands: a size 2 from one brand may differ from another's. If there is no number, look at the gap (the distance between the point and the shank).
medidas: Choose the size by the fish's mouth and the size of the bait, not by the size of the fish.
The bait must leave the point free: if it covers it, the hook is too small for that bait.
usos_costa: Small baits (thin worm, bits of prawn): high numbers (6–8).
Medium baits for white seabream, gilthead bream or bass: around 2 to 1/0 in commercial rigs.

pasarse: Size is chosen by the fish's mouth and by the bait, not by what the fish weighs. A 2 kg gilthead bream has a small mouth and is caught on a small hook; what changes with weight is the wire thickness (a «strong» or 2X hook of the same size), not the number.

A hook that is too big does not fit fully into the fish's mouth: it bites, feels the metal and drops it, or does not even take it. With live bait it is worse: the weight of the hook stops it swimming and the hole kills it sooner.
Going a little too small can be fixed (more bites, the odd one gets away); going too big leaves the rig with no bites. If in doubt, one size smaller.
Quick rule: the bait has to cover the hook, leaving the point free. If you need a huge bait to cover the hook, the hook is too big.

fichas.nombre: Swivels: which one to use when
fichas.para: Quick guide to choosing between the types of swivel.
fichas.resumen: A swivel joins two lengths of line and lets them turn separately, so the line doesn't twist. There are five families and each has its place: you don't need the most expensive one for everything.
como_es: Barrel: the basic one. Joins main line and rig or holds the lead. Turns little under load.
Rolling (ring type): the most used at sea. Turns better than the barrel and is stronger for its small size.
Ball-bearing: turns freely even under heavy load. For anything that spins a lot: spinners, trolling, baits that spin.
With snap or clip: any of the above with a clip to change lure, lead or rig without cutting.
Three-way (T): three eyes; for snoods and multi-hook rigs.
medidas: Choose the smallest one that matches the breaking strain of the rig (or a little more).
Sizes are not the same across brands: check the kilos on the pack, not the number.
For trolling, it should hold at least 1.5 times the line's strength.
usos_costa: Surfcasting: rolling swivel with snap for the lead, and rolling or three-way swivels for the snoods.
Spinning: snap only (no swivel) with swimming lures; rolling or ball-bearing swivel with spinners.
Float fishing: small rolling swivel between main line and leader, which also acts as a stop for the shot.
usos_embarcacion: Anchored and drift fishing: three-way or rolling swivels on snood rigs.
Trolling: ball-bearing swivel with snap; this is where the line twists most.
fichas.ojo: A swivel is also a weak point and a flash the fish can see: use one only where needed and just the right size.

fichas.nombre: Spinning lures: which one for the sea conditions
fichas.para: Which lure family to use depending on the state of the sea.
fichas.resumen: The state of the sea decides: in calm, clear water, surface lures and light soft plastics; in foam and rough sea, lures that grip the water or get down below the foam.
como_es: Calm sea and clear water: stickbait, small popper, floating minnow or unweighted soft plastic.
Rough sea with foam: a minnow that “bites” the water, sinking pencil, soft plastic on a jig head or a somewhat larger stickbait.
Headwind: sinking pencil or casting jig, which fly and cut through the wind.
Coloured (murky) water: white soft plastics or lures with a strong silhouette at different depths; very noisy surface lures usually do poorly.
Very rocky or weedy ground in calm conditions: unweighted soft plastic rigged weedless.
medidas: 9 to 15 cm and 10 to 30 g covers almost all shore fishing for bass.
More weight if it's windy or you need to reach far; less if the fish are tight to the shore.
usos_costa: Bass on rock and beach: the basic box is a stickbait, a minnow, a sinking pencil and a couple of soft plastics with heads of different weights.
Mackerel, bluefish and Atlantic bonito: casting jig or spinner.
usos_embarcacion: Spinning under birds (mackerel, Atlantic bonito, bluefish): casting jig or sinking pencil.
Casting at the rocks from a boat: the same as from the shore.
fichas.ojo: No lure works every time: if nothing happens in half an hour, change lure family before colour.

fichas.nombre: The rod: parts and how to read its specs
fichas.para: What each part of a rod is and what the numbers printed on it mean.
fichas.resumen: Every rod has the same parts: the blank, the guides, the reel seat and the handle. What changes between a surfcasting rod and a jigging rod is the length, power, action and casting weight.
como_es: Blank: the rod's tube (carbon, fibreglass or a mix). Carbon is lighter and more sensitive; fibreglass is tougher against knocks.
Guides (rings): carry the line; the inner ring must be smooth, with no cracks.
Reel seat: where the reel screws in; different for spinning or overhead reels.
Handle: cork or EVA; long on casting rods for leverage.
Tip: the last section; shows the bite.
Power: the force needed to bend it (light, medium, heavy): set by the size of the fish and the line.
Action: where it bends. Fast: only the tip (sensitive, sets the hook quickly). Moderate or slow: bends right down (more forgiving, cushions more).
Casting weight (e.g. 10–40 g or 100–200 g): the weight of lure or lead it casts well. Outside that range it casts badly or can break.
Sections: spigot/put-in joints (better action) or telescopic (easy to carry).
medidas: Long rod: casts further. Short: more accurate and more power to fight.
The rod's casting weight must cover your lures or leads.
usos_costa: Surfcasting: long and powerful.
Spinning: medium and sensitive.
usos_embarcacion: Boat: shorter and more powerful.
fichas.ojo: Don't cast above the casting weight marked on the rod: it's the most common way to break it.

fichas.para: Types of reel and what each spec means: size, ratio and drag.
fichas.resumen: At sea two are mainly used: the spinning reel, easy and universal, and the overhead (multiplier) reel, stronger for boat fishing and trolling.
como_es: Spinning (fixed spool): the spool doesn't turn; the line comes off the front. The easiest, and the one used for surfcasting and spinning.
Overhead (multiplier, “boat reel”): the spool turns; more power and stamina for boat fishing, heavy jigging and trolling.
Spool: holds the line; surfcasting spools are long and tapered to cast far.
Drag: lets line out when the fish pulls harder than the line can take. Front (finer and stronger) or rear.
Ratio (e.g. 5.7:1): turns of the rotor per turn of the handle. But how much line you retrieve also depends on the spool diameter.
Bail arm (pick-up): the arm that winds the line onto a spinning reel.
medidas: Size (1000, 2500, 4000, 10000…) is not the same across brands; within a brand, a higher number is bigger.
In the specs, look at the maximum drag and the line capacity.
usos_costa: Spinning: medium-sized spinning reel.
Surfcasting: large long-spool spinning reel.
usos_embarcacion: Heavy jigging, deep bottom fishing and trolling: overhead reel or large saltwater spinning reel.
fichas.ojo: At sea, it must be a reel built for salt water: freshwater reels corrode in no time.

fichas.nombre: Reel size: when to use a 2500, a 3000, a 5000…
fichas.para: Which size of spinning reel to choose for each type of fishing.
fichas.resumen: The reel's number indicates its size and how much line it holds. Rule of thumb: smaller the finer the line and the lighter the lures; bigger for long casting, thick lines and hard-pulling fish.
como_es: Within a brand, higher number = bigger reel, more line and more drag.
Across brands it's not the same: one brand's 4000 can be quite a bit smaller than another's. Compare line capacity and maximum drag.
Daiwa standardised its LT sizes (spool diameter) as 1000, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000 and 6000.
The reel must balance the rod: a very big reel on a light rod tires your wrist.

fichas.nombre: The reel drag: how to set it
fichas.para: How tight to set the drag so you don't snap the line or lose the fish.
fichas.resumen: The general rule is to set it to roughly a quarter of the line's breaking strain (or the leader's, if it's weaker). With braid, a bit less.
como_es: Measure it with a spring balance (or luggage scale), pulling the line through the guides with the rod bent.
With nylon: around 20 % of the line's strength on fine lines and 25–30 % on heavy lines.
With braid: less (15 to 25 %), because it doesn't stretch and the full shock gets through.
Calculate it on the weakest link: the leader, the knot or the rod.
medidas: Example: 10 kg leader → drag around 2–2.5 kg.
usos_costa: Spinning with fine braid: light drag, the leader is the limit.
Surfcasting: a bit tighter to set the hook at distance, without overdoing it.
usos_embarcacion: Jigging and trolling: set it before you start and don't adjust it blindly with a fish on.
fichas.ojo: Don't tighten the drag by hand while the fish is pulling: that's when most lines break. Sources disagree on whether to back it off when storing the reel.

fichas.para: How to look after your tackle after sea fishing so it lasts for years.
fichas.resumen: Salt is the enemy: a gentle rinse with fresh water after every trip, drying well and a drop of lubricant prevent almost all breakdowns.
como_es: After every trip: rinse rod and reel with gentle fresh water, as a light shower or with a cloth. Never with a pressure jet or submerged: that drives the salt inside.
Dry everything well before storing; don't store it in a wet bag.
Check the guides: run a cotton bud round them; if it catches, there's a crack that will cut the line.
Clean the reel seat, where salt builds up.
Now and then, a thin coat of anti-corrosion protector or lubricant on the external metal parts (never on the drag).
Once a year, a reel service at a shop, or strip it down yourself if you know how.
medidas: Rinse: every trip. Full service: once a year (or sooner if it's noisy or turns stiffly).
usos_costa: After beach fishing, the sand: also rinse the reel's bail arm and rotor.
usos_embarcacion: On a boat, spray gets on everything all day: always rinse when you get back.
fichas.ojo: Don't use strong soap or solvents on the reel: they remove the grease inside. And don't put oil on the drag.

Large spinning reel with a long, tapered spool (long cast).
Fine main line to fly further and a shock leader to take the strain of the cast.

fichas.resumen: Light, sensitive rod with a medium spinning reel and braid: you'll cast thousands of times, so weight matters.

Medium spinning reel with a good drag.
Fine braid with a fluorocarbon leader.

fichas.ojo: A very stiff rod with light lures doesn't load and casts short: match the casting weight to what you use most.

como_es: Short, strong rod; slow or moderate action so the fish takes the lure before it feels the rod.
High-capacity overhead reel with lever or star drag.
Rod holders on the boat: the rod works on its own until the strike.

fichas.para: A prawn-shaped lure with a crown of barbless pins at the tail, for squid and cuttlefish.
fichas.resumen: Cast it, let it sink and make it dart with sharp lifts: squid attack it as it falls. It is the way to catch squid from harbours and rocks.
como_es: Prawn-shaped body, often cloth-covered; a crown of barbless pins behind.
There are sinking (standard), floating and slow-sinking «shallow» models for shallow water.
Sizes are numbers (2.5, 3.0, 3.5…): a 2.5 is about 7.5 cm long and a 3.5 about 10.5 cm.
Sink rate is given in seconds per metre (standard models, about 3–3.5 s/m).
medidas: 2.5: small squid, shallow and calm water.
3.0: the most used all-rounder.
3.5: deeper water, current or big squid.
Check the weight and sink rate on the packet: they vary a lot between models.
usos_costa: At night under harbour and breakwater lights, or at dawn and dusk.
Cast, count it down, make two or three sharp lifts and let it fall again on a slack line.
usos_embarcacion: Slow drifting or anchored over sand and weed.
With lights at night, where allowed.
fichas.ojo: Your rod must handle the jig's weight. Carry different colours: the one that works changes from day to day.

fichas.resumen: The traditional way to catch squid from a boat: the jig is lifted and dropped vertically, often with a light at night. In Spain, «calamar de potera» means squid caught this way, one by one.
como_es: Long body (often glow-in-the-dark) with crowns of barbless pins.
Barbless pins don't damage the squid and keep it whole.
Several can be rigged on the same line, spaced apart.
medidas: Weight according to depth and current.

fichas.para: A rig with several hooks dressed with feathers or shiny strips, with a lead or a jig at the end.
fichas.resumen: The classic way to catch mackerel and horse mackerel when they come in shoals: it imitates a small shoal of fish. The sabiki is the version with smaller hooks.
como_es: Feathers: 3 to 6 dressed hooks about 30 cm apart.
Sabiki: 6 to 10 small hooks, for small horse mackerel, sardine or bogue.
At the end, a lead or, better, a small bright jig.
A glow stick on the rig helps from a pier at night.
medidas: Lead or jig of about 28 to 113 g depending on depth and current.
Big feathers for mackerel; sabiki for horse mackerel and small baitfish.
usos_costa: From a pier or harbour: cast and retrieve with up-and-down lifts, like a shoal of fish.
Or straight down: drop to the bottom and lift in jerks, about 2–3 m below the surface if the fish are up high.
usos_embarcacion: Drop to the bottom controlling the line with your thumb and lift in jerks.
Boat rod and reel with a lead of about 110 g.
fichas.ojo: Many hooks together tangle and snag on the pier wall. Respect minimum sizes and don't take more than you will use.

Big-lipped minnows for slower, deeper trolling.

fichas.nombre: Surfcasting set-up with a shock leader
fichas.para: The full surfcasting line: thin main line on the reel, a thick length (shock leader) that takes the cast, and then the rig and lead.
fichas.resumen: The basis of any cast with a heavy lead from the beach: the thin main line flies further and the shock leader takes the force of the cast.
como_es: Thin main line on the spool: it casts further.
Shock leader: a length of much stronger line, joined to the main line with a joining knot (for example the Albright or the double uni).
A swivel at the end of the leader: you can change rigs in a moment.
From the swivel hangs whichever rig you need (paternoster, running ledger, pulley…) with its lead.
With a braid main line, the leader also protects the braid from rubbing on rocks and shells, and your hands when landing the fish.
medidas: General rule: about 10 lb of breaking strain for every ounce (28 g) of lead. With 4 oz (about 113 g), at least 40 lb; with 6 oz (about 170 g), at least 60 lb.
Typical beach values: 12–20 lb main line and 50–80 lb leader.
Length: the length of the rod plus about six turns on the spool. Other guides give 2–3 rod lengths plus 4–5 turns (about 6–9 m).
usos_costa: Beach surfcasting with heavy leads and long casts.
Shingle or shelly beaches: the leader stands up to abrasion better than a thin main line.
If a tangle forces you to cut the main line, re-tie the join and get back to fishing with the same rig.
usos_embarcacion: Also used when casting from a boat (uptiding): 40–50 lb leader on a 20–25 lb main line.
pasos: Fill the spool with the main line.
Join the shock leader to the main line with a joining knot; wet both lines before tightening.
Tie a swivel to the end of the leader.
Clip the rig and lead to the swivel.
Before every cast, check that the joining knot is on the spool, with several turns of leader over it.
fichas.ojo: The leader must reach the reel with turns to spare: if the thin main line takes the cast, it can snap and send the lead flying. Never cast with people behind you or alongside.

fichas.para: A rig where the baited hook is clipped to a bait clip or impact shield next to the lead during the cast.
fichas.resumen: For casting as far as possible on clean sandy beaches: the rig flies tucked up and the bait reaches the bottom intact.
como_es: The hook is clipped to a bait clip or impact shield (a plastic piece) above the lead.
When you cast, the whole rig flies together and tucked up: more aerodynamic, fewer tangles.
On hitting the water, the shield protects the bait and releases the hook.
The shield is held with an adjustable stop (silicone or rubber tubing), not a fixed crimp: that way you set it exactly where the hook reaches.
Usually single-hook; there is also a two-hook version for big baits (see Pennell rig).
medidas: Single-hook example: 60 lb rig body, 30 lb snood and a size 2/0 hook.
Beach paternosters can also carry 2 or 3 clips so they are not too long to cast.
usos_costa: Sandy beaches where the fish feed far out and you need distance.
Clean ground, with no rocks.
Powerful (pendulum) casts: the tucked-up rig stands the cast better.
fichas.ojo: Clean ground only: on rocks it snags. And before every cast check that the hook is properly held in the clip, or the bait will fly off.

fichas.para: Two hooks on the same snood, one at each end of a big bait.
fichas.resumen: For big baits (whole squid, mackerel fillet, big worm baits): the fish is hooked whichever end it takes.
como_es: The bottom hook is tied at the end of the snood.
The top hook sits further up the same snood, at whatever distance the bait needs.
Sliding top hook: wrap the snood round the shank, or hold it with a piece of silicone tubing (about 2 mm), and move it to suit the bait.
Fixed top hook: tie it on with a snell knot; it won't move, but the bait always has to be the same size.
Hooks with an up-turned eye are easier to thread.
medidas: Big, strong hooks, because it is for big fish. In one clipped-down example, two size 4/0.
Some anglers prefer both the same; others make the top one at least one size smaller. Both work.
usos_costa: With a pulley (pulley Pennell) on rocky, snaggy ground, for big fish.
Clipped down (see clipped-down rig) on sandy or shingle beaches for distance.
Big fish: bass, rays or conger eel.
usos_embarcacion: When casting from a boat (uptiding), a single snood with Pennell hooks is the most popular choice for big fish.
fichas.ojo: With a sliding top hook, if a big fish pulls on the head of the bait, the hook can slide down to the bottom one. Always clip big baits down: loose, they flap during the cast and tangle.

fichas.para: A small live fish hung under a sliding float, with a lead that keeps it at the chosen depth.
fichas.resumen: Widely used for bass, and also for pollack and other predators, next to rocks and breakwaters.
como_es: It is the sliding float rig (see «Float rig»), with a drilled lead under the float that keeps the livebait down.
Between the lead and the hook, a 60–90 cm snood: the livebait swims below the lead.
A float with plenty of buoyancy for the lead and bait; bubble floats are popular for livebaiting.
Where to hook it: through the nose or lip, it swims more naturally and copes with current; through the back near the tail, it tends to swim down and away.
For bass on livebait, some anglers swap the single hook for a treble.
medidas: Hook size 1 to 4/0, depending on the size of the livebait: match the hook to the bait, not to the fish you're after. Too big a hook kills its life and action.
10–20 lb snood, clear nylon or fluorocarbon.
Depth: start a few metres down and go deeper until you find the fish; big pollack tend to be deeper.
usos_costa: Bass next to rocks, breakwaters and groynes: let the tide carry the float slowly.
Pollack deeper down, close to the rock face.
usos_embarcacion: The same rig works from a boat, at anchor or on the drift.
fichas.ojo: Don't strike at the first touch: wait until the float goes right under. If you miss, leave it out: the fish often comes back. Before fishing with live fish as bait, check the rules where you are: each region or country may have its own.

fichas.nombre: Weak link for the lead (rotten bottom)
fichas.para: A length of line weaker than the rest between the rig and the lead, so that if the lead snags only that piece breaks.
fichas.resumen: On rocks and wrecks you lose the lead but get the rig back and, often, the fish.
como_es: The lead isn't tied to the rig with the same line: it hangs on a short length of weaker line.
When the lead snags, you pull and the weak link breaks; the rest comes up.
From a boat there's no cast: just tie the lead with weaker line to a swivel or to the leg of the boom.
From the shore, the lead sits in a clip or link that holds it during the cast and releases it when it hits the water, leaving it hanging on the weak link.
There are plastic links with a lock that opens on hitting the water; the lead stays attached and breaks free if it snags.
medidas: Weak link of about 10–15 lb (12–15 lb in the boat example), always weaker than the main line and the rig.
From a boat a length of about 7–8 cm is enough; a cable tie or a paper clip also works.
usos_costa: Rocks and rough ground, with a plain lead.
Conger fishing among rocks and at the foot of stone piers.
usos_embarcacion: Bottom fishing over rock or wrecks: with bottom rigs, conger rigs or booms.
fichas.ojo: Weak-link rigs are not for power (pendulum) casting: the lead can come off mid-cast. Cast gently overhead. If the link has a plastic lock, re-set it every time you reel in.

fichas.para: A stiff wire arm (boom) on the main line: the lead hangs from its leg and a long trace with a soft lure or bait comes off its tip.
fichas.resumen: For pollack and coalfish over rock and wrecks from a boat: the boom drops fast without the long trace tangling.
como_es: Stiff wire boom (French-boom type): plastic ones flex under water pressure and tangle.
The main line goes to the top eye of the boom; the lead to its leg, on a weak link.
The long clear mono trace goes to the eye at the tip, with a swivel halfway along to stop twist.
At the end, an eel-type soft lure (or a bait).
Optional: a thicker, stiffer upper half to the trace, so it tangles less at slack water.
medidas: Boom of at least 10 inches (about 25 cm) on reefs; 15 inches (about 38 cm) on deep wrecks.
Trace: about 10–12 ft (3–3.7 m) on reefs around 100 ft (30 m) deep; on wrecks deeper than 150 ft (45 m), at least 12 ft and typically 15–18 ft (4.5–5.5 m).
15–20 lb main line; 12–18 lb trace; 12–15 lb weak link.
usos_embarcacion: Pollack and coalfish over wrecks and reefs, on the drift.
Hopper variant (long boom and a short 4–6 ft trace of 30–50 lb with a weighted shad) for working tight to the bottom: ling and cod.
In summer, bass over shallower wrecks.
pasos: Let the rig drop until the lead touches bottom.
Engage the reel and lift the lead a few feet off the bottom or the wreck.
Pause a few seconds so the trace straightens out behind the boom.
Retrieve at slow to medium speed, counting the turns of the handle: when they bite, you know the depth the fish are at.
Don't strike at the first touch: keep winding until the rod pulls right over; the fish hooks itself.
fichas.ojo: If you get plucks that don't hook up (they're nipping the lure's tail), lengthen the trace before changing colour.

fichas.para: A short, very heavy running ledger rig with one big hook and strong swivels.
fichas.resumen: Conger eels have teeth, live among rocks and wrecks and spin as they come up: the rig has to cope with all three.
como_es: Running lead on a slider boom, between two beads, on a length of heavy mono that protects the main line from abrasion.
Below that, a strong swivel and the hook length of very heavy mono or steel wire (see «Steel wire»).
A single big hook.
The lead on a weak link (see «Weak link for the lead»): it snags a lot on that ground.
Little metalwork: fewer things to snag.
medidas: Boat: braid main line; 24 in (60 cm) of 100 lb mono for the boom; 30 in (75 cm) hook length of 200 lb mono; 8/0 hook on reefs or 10/0 on wrecks with very big conger.
Shore: 30 lb main line; 100 lb wire or 100 lb-plus mono hook length; 6/0 or 8/0 hook; 10–15 lb weak link.
usos_costa: Rock crevices, rough ground and the base of stone piers: lower the rig straight down or lob it a short way, no power casting.
Reel in free spool with the ratchet on, so the conger can take line without dragging the lead.
usos_embarcacion: Reefs and wrecks, at anchor: 8/0 hook on reefs and 10/0 on wrecks.
Straight braid, no shock leader: better feel and more pressure.
fichas.ojo: Conger spin as they come up: use big, good-quality swivels between the hook length and the main line, or the line will twist and break.

fichas.para: A long trace dragged along the bottom with the boat on the drift, with coloured beads and sometimes a spoon that stirs up the sand.
fichas.resumen: For plaice, flounder and turbot over sand: flatfish are drawn to colour and movement.
como_es: Running ledger: a slider boom with the lead on the main line, a bead and a swivel.
A long fluorocarbon trace comes off the swivel: it stands up better to abrasion on shell.
Next to the hook, 5 or 6 coloured beads (green and black, or yellow and red).
Spoon variant: a long trace to a revolving spoon and, behind it, a short hook length with beads and the hook.
Buttlöffel variant: a figure-of-eight lead spoon acts as the weight, stirs up the bottom and flutters on the drop; it carries two snoods above it.
medidas: Running ledger: 4–6 ft (1.2–1.8 m) of 12–20 lb fluorocarbon; size 1 Aberdeen hook.
With a spoon: 5–10 ft (1.5–3 m) of 10 lb from the swivel to the spoon and about 6 in (15 cm) from the spoon to the hook; Aberdeen size 2 to 2/0.
Buttlöffel: 30–90 g; the lightest that keeps contact with the bottom. Snoods of about 45 cm of 10–20 lb.
usos_costa: The buttlöffel can also be fished from the beach in shallower water, roving along the shoreline.
On clean sandy beaches at short range, with short-snood paternosters, beads and a size 1 hook.
usos_embarcacion: Slow drifts over clean sand: the spoon flutters and draws attention.
In slack tide, a shorter trace, close to 1.5 m.
fichas.ojo: Use the lightest lead or spoon that keeps contact with the bottom in the tide and drift there is. From the beach, several flapping hooks cut casting distance and snag more.

fichas.para: From an anchored boat, you cast the rig uptide with a grip lead, away from the hull, and leave it anchored on the bottom.
fichas.resumen: In shallow water, boat noise scares fish feeding underneath; casting away finds them where they're undisturbed. It also needs less lead in strong tides.
como_es: A rod rather longer than a boat rod, with a casting reel (not a big downtide winch).
20–25 lb mono main line with a 40–50 lb shock leader.
Grip lead: fixed wires in strong tides, breakout wires in weaker flow.
Simple rigs: a single snood, often with Pennell hooks for big fish. Long-snood boom rigs tangle.
medidas: Rods of about 9 ft 6 in–10 ft (2.9–3 m) casting about 4–8 oz (113–227 g).
Mainly used in about 60 ft (18 m) of water or less.
usos_embarcacion: At anchor in shallow water with tide: big bottom fish that keep away from the boat.
When there's no room to let every rig out downtide without tangling.
pasos: Get the lead and trace outside the boat before you start the cast.
Cast gently, overhead or underarm; add power as you get the hang of it.
When the lead hits bottom, keep paying out line: the tide forms a bow that digs the grip lead in.
Pay out until the line is about 45° downtide of where you cast. On a new venue, pay out double what you think.
Rest the rod against the side of the boat and wait.
Bite: the rod tip nods and then springs back (the fish has dislodged the lead). Pick up the rod, wind quickly to take up the slack and, once you feel the weight, lift: no strike is needed.
fichas.ojo: On a boat with other people, never start the cast with the lead and hooks inside: get them over the side first, then cast. If you pay out too little line or the lead is too light, it will pull free and wash away with the tide.

fichas.para: A heavy piece of metal with assist hooks that is dropped vertically from the boat and worked up with snaps or at full speed.
fichas.resumen: For active fish, in mid-water or under bait schools, over rock and wrecks. Many bites come on the drop.
como_es: Long and slim (knife style): sinks fast and slides sideways; short and wide: flutters more.
Tail-weighted: sinks fast. Centre-weighted: flutters and moves more from side to side.
Assist hooks on a solid ring (see “Assist hook (jigging)”).
Zero-stretch braid and a high-speed reel (see “Jigging outfit (boat)”).
medidas: There is no fixed rule: the lightest jig that reaches the bottom and keeps the line almost vertical.
One source's starting point: 1 g per foot of depth (about 3 g per metre). More current or more drift, more weight.
If the line angles more than about 15°, use a heavier jig.
usos_costa: From the shore you use a casting jig: see “Casting jig”.
usos_embarcacion: Over rock, wrecks and bottom changes marked on the sounder.
Under bait schools, for fish hunting in mid-water.
One guide lists it for common dentex, greater amberjack, groupers, red porgy, little tunny, dolphinfish and bluefish.
pasos: Get over the marks on the sounder and drop the jig to the bottom.
Make rod snaps of 30 to 60 cm and let the jig fall on an almost slack line.
Another way: wind at full speed through the marked zone, with the odd pause after a few turns.
Watch the line on the drop: a tap or sudden slack is a bite.
When the jig has passed the fish zone, drop it back down.
fichas.ojo: Tie the leader directly to the solid ring, not to a split ring: a split ring can open with a big fish.

fichas.para: An asymmetric metal jig that is lifted a little at a time with the rod and allowed to flutter down like a wounded fish.
fichas.resumen: A finesse technique, mainly for bottom fish, that is less tiring than speed jigging. Most bites come on the drop.
como_es: Asymmetric and centre-weighted.
Short and wide: falls more slowly and flutters more; for shallower water and sluggish fish (short pitch).
Long and slim: falls faster, with a tighter action; for deeper water and active fish (long pitch).
A very light, soft rod that springs back and pitches the jig; thin braid so the line drops vertically.
medidas: Shallow water: 60 g or less.
Deeper grounds: 90 to 120 g.
Great depths or big offshore fish: 300 g or more.
usos_costa: From the shore you use a casting jig: see “Casting jig”.
usos_embarcacion: Bottom fish over rock and wrecks.
Also mid-water predators that come down to feed near the bottom.
Two experts in one magazine say it works best from about 45 m of depth.
pasos: Drop the jig to the bottom with a little tension so it falls vertically.
Rest the rod butt under your forearm.
Lift the rod just enough to load it, then stop: the tip springs back and pitches the jig up. A sharp turn of the handle with the rod still also works.
Lower the tip and follow the fall with slack line: that is what makes the jig flutter.
Don't wind during the drop and watch the line: that is where most bites come.
Work the lower part, about 5–9 m off the bottom.
fichas.ojo: When fighting the fish, keep the rod parallel to the water or lower: above that it can break. Gain line with the reel, not the rod.

fichas.para: A jig with a bullet-shaped metal body and a soft octopus or squid skirt, with assist hooks.
fichas.resumen: The body sinks fast and the skirt moves on its own: it needs little rod work. For bottom-hugging or cautious fish that feed slowly.
como_es: Compact, heavy metal body.
Soft octopus or squid style skirt, which must move freely.
Assist hooks hanging loose, separate from the body.
It swims better with the line at a slight angle than straight up and down.
medidas: 40 to 80 g: shallow water or light drift.
80 to 150 g: medium depth or moderate current.
150 to 300 g or more: deep water or strong current.
If the line sweeps far from the boat, go up in weight before changing colour.
usos_embarcacion: Fish holding on the bottom or not chasing a fast jig.
One guide lists it for common dentex, greater amberjack, groupers and red porgy on rock and drop-offs.
pasos: Let it sink to the bottom or to the depth marked on the sounder.
Take up the slack.
Wind at a steady pace and vary the speed to see what the fish want.
If needed, the odd short lift or pause, with no hard snaps.
Each time it touches bottom, lift it a little and work just above to avoid snagging.
fichas.ojo: Check the skirt before every drop: torn, stiff or tangled in the hooks, it does not work. And don't work it like a speed jig: the skirt stops moving.

fichas.para: A lead head that slides freely on the line, with coloured skirts and rubber tendrils and two small, strong hooks.
fichas.resumen: Wound in slowly and steadily, with no jerks. Designed for sea bream (“tai” in Japanese); also used for groupers.
como_es: Weighted head that slides freely on the line.
Long, slim, coloured skirts and tendrils that move on the retrieve.
Among the tendrils, an assist rig with two small but strong hooks.
The leader-to-mainline knot acts as a stop so the tendrils don't slide too far up.
medidas: In 35–50 m, New Zealand charter skippers start at 140 g and go to 180 g if the wind or current picks up.
A weight that gets down and stays there; if in doubt, go heavier.
Slow retrieve: half a turn to two turns of the handle per second.
usos_embarcacion: New Zealand snapper, kingfish and john dory, in 20–100 m (best 30–50 m).
Sea bream and groupers in shallow water (up to about 60 m, per one source).
If the bite is slow, a small strip of squid tentacle on the leading hook.
pasos: Drift-fish; if the drift is too fast, use a drift sock.
Lob the lure a little ahead of the boat so it reaches the bottom sooner.
When it touches bottom, engage the reel.
Wind slowly for about 3–6 m of line; if nothing bites, drop it back down.
If you feel taps, don't strike: keep winding at the same pace or a bit faster and the fish hooks itself.
When the line reaches about 35–40°, wind in and start another drift.
fichas.ojo: Don't strike at the first tap, keep winding. And avoid very rough ground: you lose a lot of tackle.

fichas.nombre: Soft plastic on a jig head from a boat
fichas.para: A soft plastic rigged on a jig head to fish it near the bottom from a boat.
fichas.resumen: Cheap and versatile: the same soft plastic fishes any depth just by changing the head weight. From a boat, vertically or on the drift.
como_es: Paddle tail (shad): swims on its own on the retrieve and on the drop; imitates a small fish.
Curl tail (grub): moves on the drop, on the retrieve and even at rest on the bottom; good for beginners.
Straight or forked tail: almost no built-in action and sinks faster; good on the bottom and offshore. You work it with the rod tip.
For vertical jigging, a straight tail usually beats a paddle tail, which can spin on the drop.
Colour: light and natural in clear water and sun; dark in dirty water or low light; fluoro if nothing works (more in “Lure colours: which to choose”).
medidas: In bays and offshore, from about 3.5 g (1/8 oz) to 85 g (3 oz); with big plastics, deep water and strong current, more.
More depth, wind or current: more weight. A plastic with a lively tail sinks more slowly.
Hook matched to the size of the plastic; heavy wire for fish with strong jaws.
usos_costa: From the shore: see “Soft plastic (soft lure)”. Same plastic, lighter heads.
usos_embarcacion: Vertical or drift fishing near the bottom, over rock and sand.
On the drift, cast downwind: the line stays vertical for longer.
Cast up-current to reach deeper with the same head.
pasos: Hold the plastic next to the head and note where the point must come out for it to sit straight.
Push the point into the centre of the plastic's nose, as if threading a worm.
Keep going through the centre of the body; if you go off centre, pull back a little and carry on.
Push the point out through the back at the spot you noted.
Slide the plastic up to the jig head and check in the water that it swims straight.
fichas.ojo: Tie the line to the jig head's eye with a direct knot, not a loop: with high pressure and thin line the loop can slip out of the eye.

fichas.para: Holding the boat still on the anchor, up-current of a specific spot, to fish over it and use groundbait.
fichas.resumen: For working a wreck or rock you have already marked and holding the fish there with chum. One skipper in a magazine only anchors if he sees bait on the sounder.
como_es: Anchor up-current of the spot: the current sets the boat over it and carries the chum to the fish.
Beforehand, a test drift over the spot tells you which way and how hard the current is pushing.
Examples from skippers in one magazine: one anchors 23–30 m up-current of the wreck; another, about 90 m.
Chum: little and steady. Throw too much and it stops working and the fish scatter.
On the bottom, sand balls with chum work: they take it down and spread the scent.
medidas: At least 3 times the depth; in rough water, 5 times.
Count from the bow, not the water: in shallow water, bow height changes the sum a lot.
usos_embarcacion: Wrecks, rocks and small reefs you want right under you.
Chum fishing for fish that need drawing in.
Bottom rigs with bait: see “Running ledger (sliding lead)”.
pasos: Make a test drift over the spot to read the current.
Move up-current and lower the anchor from the bow, don't throw it, so it doesn't tangle.
Pay out rode (at least 3 times the depth) and make it fast at the bow.
Check it is holding: rode tension and your position against landmarks.
If you have marked fish, chum for about half an hour before fishing and keep it going little and often.
Check now and then that the anchor is not dragging.
fichas.ojo: Never anchor from the stern or the side: the boat can be swamped. Also see “Where not to anchor”.

fichas.para: Letting the wind and current carry the boat, with the engine off or in neutral, while the rigs work the bottom.
fichas.resumen: You cover a lot of ground and find fish. Speed is what matters: not so fast that the rig skips, not so slow that it goes dead.
como_es: Good speed in most cases: half a knot to one and a half knots.
Wind and current the same way: a clean drift. Opposed: the boat slows or stops and there are usually fewer bites.
To slow down: a drift sock, especially when the wind pushes harder than the current. To fine-tune: bump the engine in and out of gear.
Line almost vertical: you're right. Far behind the boat: too fast or not enough lead. Straight down and not moving: too slow.
medidas: The lightest that keeps the rig on the bottom.
One guide says deeper water may need 8 to 12 ounces (about 225–340 g) to keep bottom contact.
usos_embarcacion: Sand and gravel ground with scattered fish.
Jigs, inchiku, tai rubber and soft plastics on the drift.
If you miss a bite, free-spool for a few seconds: the fish sometimes comes back.
pasos: Read the wind and current and choose a drift that crosses structure: edges, humps, depressions, wrecks or rock.
Get up-current (or upwind) of the spot and put the engine in neutral.
Drop the rig to the bottom and watch the line angle.
Adjust speed (drift sock or engine) and lead until the line is almost vertical.
If you get a bite, mark the spot or save the GPS track and repeat the same drift.
fichas.ojo: Fish often stack up in small areas near structure: a few metres off on the drift can change the day. Repeat the good one.

fichas.para: A fabric cone streamed in the water on a line from the boat to slow the drift.
fichas.resumen: So the rig moves more slowly and spends more time over good ground when the wind is pushing too hard.
como_es: A wide-mouthed cone open at the narrow end: water goes in the mouth, out the back, and slows the boat.
Tow line tied to the bridle at the mouth.
Retrieval (dump) line on the narrow end: pulling it collapses the cone so it comes in easily.
Streamed off the bow or the side.
medidas: Makers give charts by boat length: use them as a starting point.
A small one slows you less but is lighter and easier to handle; if you use it a lot, carry two sizes.
usos_embarcacion: A drift that is too fast in the wind, especially when the wind pushes harder than the current.
Tai rubber, inchiku and bottom rigs that need to go slowly.
With the GPS on: if a drift produces fish, repeat the same track.
fichas.ojo: Fit a large float: if it comes loose, it sinks at once and is gone.

fichas.nombre: Choosing the spot with the sounder
fichas.para: Using the sounder to find hard bottom, rock and bottom changes before anchoring or starting the drift.
fichas.resumen: Bottom fish are usually on hard ground and structure. The sounder tells you whether there is rock or sand below.
como_es: Thick bottom band (strong echo): hard bottom, such as rock or reef. Thin band (weak echo): soft bottom, such as sand or mud.
Thin second echo: soft bottom. Wider, darker second echo: hard bottom (rock or rubble).
Hard bottom may have little relief and still hold bait and fish.
Low frequencies (50 kHz) show the type of bottom better.
usos_embarcacion: Find edges, humps, depressions, wrecks and rock to cross on the drift.
Anchor only when you see bait or fish over the spot.
Mark the spots where you get bites on the GPS so you can go back.
pasos: Set a depth range a little over double the depth (in 15 m of water, about 33 m).
Turn off the clutter filter, raise the gain until a clear second echo appears, then back it off a touch.
Run over the area and watch the thickness of the bottom and the second echo.
When the bottom changes or you see fish, mark the spot.
Readjust the gain whenever the depth changes a lot.
fichas.ojo: Gain does not add power: it only filters what you see. And if the frequency cannot reach that depth, more gain fixes nothing.

fichas.nombre: Where not to anchor (and signals at anchor)
fichas.para: What the official rules say about where to avoid anchoring and how to signal a boat at anchor.
fichas.resumen: Don't anchor in channels or traffic lanes, or on protected seagrass meadows. Each region and each protected area may have its own rules.
como_es: International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs), rule 9(g): whenever possible, avoid anchoring in a narrow channel.
COLREGs, rule 10(g): avoid anchoring in a traffic separation scheme or in areas near its ends.
COLREGs, rule 30: at anchor, one ball forward by day; at night, an all-round white light (under 50 m in length, one is enough).
Under 7 m in length it is not compulsory unless you are in or near a narrow channel, an anchorage or where other vessels normally navigate.
Balearic Islands (Decree 25/2018, art. 7): anchoring on Posidonia seagrass is generally prohibited; over it, only with low-impact systems (authorised buoys).
usos_embarcacion: Anchor on sand or rock, away from harbour entrance channels and traffic lanes.
Marine reserves, parks and other protected areas may have their own rules: check them before you go.
Use the regulated mooring buoy fields where there are any.
fichas.ojo: This is not the whole of the rules: each region, port and protected area may have its own. Check the official rules for your area.

fichas.para: The gun that fires the shaft: either with rubber bands you stretch or with pressurised air inside.
fichas.resumen: The band gun is the simplest and most common; the pneumatic gives a lot of power for its size but needs more maintenance.
como_es: Band gun: one or more rubber bands that you stretch and hook onto the shaft. It is the simplest and cheapest to maintain.
With a band gun you change the power by adding or removing bands, and it fires almost silently.
Bands wear out: replace them before they deteriorate, because an old band is dangerous.
Pneumatic: the shaft sits inside a sealed barrel with air that you pump by hand. Lots of power for its size.
A pneumatic gun loses power the deeper you go and needs more maintenance.
medidas: Spearguns are usually between 0.5 and 2 m long.
A Euro-style band gun has an effective range of about three times the shaft length, measured from the tip of the gun.
fichas.ojo: Never carry the gun loaded out of the water: it is dangerous and banned in Spain (RD 347/2011, art. 16) and Portugal (Portaria 14/2014, art. 3). Keep the safety on except when you are about to shoot.

fichas.nombre: Speargun length: match it to the water
fichas.para: How to choose how long your speargun should be.
fichas.resumen: Visibility decides: murky water and rock, short gun; clear water and fish in open water, long gun.
como_es: In poor visibility the fish appears close: you need a short, manoeuvrable gun.
In clear water the fish sees you from far away and shots are longer: a long gun, more accurate at distance, works best.
For rock fish that dart into holes and caves, go short: you have to aim quickly before they hide.
With fish swimming in open water you have more time to aim, so manoeuvrability matters less.
A short gun moves better among rocks and is easier for beginners; a long one has more power but is less agile.
Bigger fish call for longer guns.
medidas: Effective range is two to three times the band stretch distance.
Length is measured from the tip of the muzzle to the back of the handle.
There is no fixed chart of centimetres per visibility: try and adjust to your area.
fichas.ojo: Don't pick the longest gun thinking you'll catch more: in murky water or among rocks a long gun is slow to swing and you'll miss shots.

fichas.nombre: Shaft and tip (Tahitian, threaded, slip tip)
fichas.para: The steel shaft the gun fires and the tip that holds the fish.
fichas.resumen: Fixed tip with a flopper for reef fish; slip tip, on a threaded shaft, for large open-water fish.
como_es: Tahitian: one-piece shaft with the tip on the shaft itself and a folding flopper that opens inside the fish. Fast and accurate, but it can sometimes pass straight through.
Threaded: the tip screws on and is changed when damaged. Short tips have one flopper; longer ones may have several.
Slip or breakaway tip: about 10–15 cm of tip separates after penetrating and stays joined to the shaft by cable or line. Recommended for large fish.
Fixed flopper tip: for reef fish. Slip tip: for open-water fish with softer flesh, which can tear off a fixed shaft and escape.
On the same gun, a threaded shaft has to be shorter than a flopper shaft.
medidas: Thin (6.5–7.5 mm): lighter, shoots further and penetrates more easily, but bends more readily on big reef fish.
Thick (8 mm): for large open-water fish.
The shaft should stick out about 23–28 cm (9–11 inches) beyond the muzzle.
fichas.ojo: Carry a spare shaft: a bent shaft with no spare ends your day.

fichas.nombre: Reel or float line on the gun
fichas.para: What links the gun to extra line or a float so you lose neither the fish nor the shaft.
fichas.resumen: A reel pays out line when the fish pulls; a float line lets you follow the fish and find your shaft. Choose by the seabed.
como_es: The shooting line wraps around the gun on loading and releases when you shoot. It should be thin, to limit drag, and strong: at least about 135 kg (300 lb).
Reel: mounted on the gun, it pays out line after the shot so you can play the fish. Useful where rock or kelp stops you towing a float.
Float line: links the gun to the float. It can be braided line, monofilament inside an airtight tube, or bungee cord.
With a float you can find your shaft in weed and recover fish that hide in holes.
If you use your marker buoy, don't move further from it than the law allows: 25 m in Spain and 30 m in Portugal (see the buoy card).
fichas.ojo: Any line in the water can tangle around you or the gun. Check it when loading and keep a knife within reach.

fichas.para: The suit that keeps you warm while you spearfish on a breath-hold.
fichas.resumen: Thickness depends on water temperature; an open-cell lining is among the warmest.
como_es: Open-cell inside: among the warmest suits. It costs more and is more fragile, and you need to lubricate it to put it on, for example with water and a little conditioner or baby powder.
Lined outside (smooth): easy to put on, dries fast and cuts wind chill, but it is damaged if you scrape it on rock.
Two-piece (jacket and trousers or long john): they overlap at the core and are warmer in cold water.
Look for a chest pad: it protects you when loading the gun.
Neoprene floats and compresses as you go down: a thick suit floats a lot at the surface and loses buoyancy at depth; a thin one changes less.
Colour: blue or blue camo in clear water; browns over rocky ground.
medidas: Warm water (24–28 °C): 1–2.5 mm.
Cool water (16–23 °C): 3–5 mm.
Very cold water: 7 mm.
fichas.ojo: If you change suit thickness, work out your weighting again: more neoprene needs more lead.

fichas.nombre: Weighting: how much lead to carry
fichas.para: The weights that offset how much your body and suit float.
fichas.resumen: Carry just enough lead to float at the surface and become neutral around 10–12 m. Overweighting is one of the factors behind blackouts.
como_es: Rubber belt with a quick-release buckle that you or your buddy can open.
As you go down, suit and lungs compress: you float less and, past the neutral point, you sink with little effort.
Most freedivers become neutral between 10 and 12 m.
You must float at the surface even after a full exhale: if you black out, your buddy has to be able to keep you up.
Be positively buoyant in the last 10 m: the end of the ascent is the hardest part.
Too much lead means very fast descents and exhausting ascents; many blackouts happen to divers who are overexerted, overweighted and unsupervised.
pasos: Put on all your gear: suit, belt and fins.
In the water, float upright and relaxed, and breathe out fully.
Check the waterline: ideally around your eyebrows.
If you sink quickly, remove lead; if you struggle to go under, add a little.
Repeat the test whenever you change suit or area.
fichas.ojo: If in doubt, go lighter on lead. And show your buddy how to release your belt.

fichas.para: The basic kit for moving and seeing underwater on a breath-hold.
fichas.resumen: Long fins to move with little effort, a low-volume mask that is easy to equalise and a simple snorkel.
como_es: Long-blade fins (up to a metre): you move further with less effort while holding your breath.
Plastic blades to start: tough and easy to travel with. Fibreglass or carbon: lighter but more fragile.
Use two fins, not a monofin: bi-fins are the ones for recreational freediving and buddy watching.
Low-volume mask: little air between lens and face. You use less air from your lungs to equalise it on the way down and avoid mask squeeze.
Snorkel: the simpler the better. It is only for breathing at the surface while you get ready.
Take the snorkel out of your mouth before you dive: on the way up you'd have to blow hard to clear it just when you need air, and if you black out it lets water in.
fichas.ojo: Never force ear equalisation: if it won't clear, go up. Forcing it can burst the eardrum or damage the inner ear.

fichas.para: The buoy that warns boats there is a diver below.
fichas.resumen: It is compulsory in Spain and Portugal and you must stay close to it. Being hit by a boat is one of the biggest risks in freediving.
como_es: Spain: every diver marks their position with a clearly visible buoy and may not move more than 25 m from it (Royal Decree 347/2011, art. 15).

Spain: outside a buoyed bathing area, breath-hold diving must be marked with a surface device: a highly visible buoy flying the International Code of Signals "Alpha" flag (Royal Decree 550/2020, arts. 2 and 5).

Spain: RD 550/2020 requires vessels to keep 50 m from diving areas, but breath-hold diving is outside that article. There is no national distance for spearfishing: check your autonomous community and the Harbour Master.

Portugal (mainland): round or cylindrical buoy, red, orange or yellow, at least 8 litres, with an Alpha flag; or a board at least 70 × 40 × 5 cm with a mast of 40 cm or more and an Alpha flag (Portaria 14/2014, art. 2).
Portugal: the buoy may not be more than 30 m from you, every vessel must keep 50 m from it, and a support boat must fly the Alpha flag (Portaria 14/2014, arts. 4 and 7).
You can carry water and spares on the buoy, and hold on to it to rest.
medidas: Spain: diver no more than 25 m from their buoy.
Portugal: diver no more than 30 m from their buoy; vessels 50 m from the buoy.
fichas.ojo: Many boats ignore the buoy, but it is the only thing that shows you are there. If you have a support boat, have it fly the Alpha flag: it greatly cuts the risk.

fichas.nombre: Line, knife and calling for help
fichas.para: The line that links you to the buoy, the knife to cut yourself free and what you need to raise the alarm.
fichas.resumen: With the line your buddy knows where you are; the knife frees you if you get tangled; a radio puts you in touch with shore.
como_es: The line links the buoy to the gun. It can be braided, monofilament inside an airtight tube, or bungee.
With the buoy and its line your buddy can follow you and always knows where you are.
Knife: for freeing yourself if you get tangled. Carry only the essentials.
To call for help, a VHF radio is best: at sea a mobile phone doesn't always have signal.
Keep a note of the emergency numbers and the VHF channel for your area.
fichas.ojo: Before you get in, agree with your buddy what each of you will do if one gets tangled or blacks out.
