fichas.nombre: Never alone: one up, one down
fichas.para: The basic freediving rule: while one dives, the other watches from above.
fichas.resumen: Almost all blackouts end well if a buddy is there to get the diver's face out of the water. Without one, they can end in drowning.
como_es: The most feared freediving accident is blackout; it almost always resolves without harm if a buddy is there to get the diver's face out of the water.
"Same ocean, same time" is not diving with a buddy: if you each fish your own way, nobody is watching.
The one at the surface does nothing but watch.
The system protects on simple dives in good visibility; the more complex the dive, the more easily it breaks down.
pasos: Before you get in, go over what each of you will do if there is a blackout or a samba.
Only one dives. The other stays at the surface, above them, watching the whole time.
When the diver comes up, the buddy goes down to meet them, at roughly a third of the depth, and comes up alongside, slightly below.
At the surface, the buddy watches the diver's face for at least another 30 seconds: some blackouts happen after surfacing.
Only swap roles once the diver who came up has recovered.
fichas.ojo: Take a freediving course with an instructor: you'll learn to rescue your buddy, and they'll learn to rescue you.

fichas.para: Losing consciousness (blackout) or body control (samba) from lack of oxygen at the end of a breath-hold.
fichas.resumen: It strikes without warning, usually near the surface on the way up or just after surfacing. What saves you is an attentive buddy.
como_es: The urge to breathe comes from CO₂, not lack of oxygen: you can run out of oxygen without feeling the need to breathe.
It usually happens near the surface, in the last 3 m of the ascent, or at the surface after coming up.
Samba: loss of motor control; the body shakes or spasms and the diver cannot control it.
Signs: slowing down, losing coordination, a dazed look, bubbles from the mouth, limp arms or legs.
Hyperventilation, fatigue, overweighting and lack of supervision all play a part.
pasos: If they black out underwater, bring them up protecting their airway: keep water out.
At the surface, keep their face out of the water.
Stimulate them with "tap, blow, talk": the method most agencies consider most effective.
If they are not breathing, they need rescue breaths and emergency help.
After a blackout or samba the day is over: stay out of the water for at least 24 hours.
fichas.ojo: It is more common than it seems: about 70% of Italian competition spearfishers had had at least one blackout. Don't stretch a breath-hold for a fish.

fichas.nombre: Breathing before and after each dive
fichas.para: How to prepare at the surface and how to recover when you come up.
fichas.resumen: Don't hyperventilate before diving; do recovery breathing when you surface and rest at the surface at least twice as long as the dive lasted.
como_es: Hyperventilating is breathing hard and fast to lower CO₂. It adds no oxygen: it only delays the urge to breathe and raises the risk of blackout.
A few forced breaths (6 or 7) are enough to hyperventilate. Calling them "cleansing breaths" changes nothing.
Two full breaths at most before diving.
If you feel tingling in your hands or face, stop your preparation and wait a few minutes.
pasos: When you start, do 3 or 4 warm-up dives, no deeper than 5 m.
At the surface, breathe calmly, using your diaphragm, at your natural pace.
Before diving, two full breaths at most, and take the snorkel out of your mouth.
On surfacing, do recovery breathing: let out part of the air, inhale quickly and briefly close your throat, holding the pressure; repeat for about 30 seconds.
Rest at the surface at least twice as long as the dive lasted, and three times as long after a deep dive.
fichas.ojo: On long days drink water even if you're not thirsty, don't dive on an empty stomach or after a heavy meal, and if you're tired, cramping or your gear fails, get out.

fichas.para: What the national law says about spearfishing in Spain's external waters.
fichas.resumen: Regional licence, breath-hold only, daylight only, gun unloaded out of the water and buoy within 25 m. Your autonomous community and each marine reserve add their own rules.
como_es: Breath-hold only: no equipment that lets you breathe underwater and no mechanical propulsion (art. 3).
You need the activity licence issued by a coastal autonomous community (or Ceuta and Melilla), and must follow the rules of the community whose coast you fish (art. 13).
Only a hand spear or a mechanically powered gun, with one or more points. Spearfishing is banned if spearfishing gear and breathing equipment are on board the same boat (art. 14).
A clearly visible marker buoy, and never more than 25 m from it (art. 15).
Banned: a loaded gun out of the water; explosive, electric or electronic tips; lights other than hand torches; underwater scooters and similar; and fishing at night, from sunset to sunrise (art. 16).

Also banned: attracting fish by any means, such as lights, except chumming with small pelagics; using poisonous, narcotic, explosive or polluting substances; and interfering with commercial fishing (arts. 12 and 16).
Only species in Annex I, at their minimum size, and never for sale (arts. 1 and 4).
medidas: To your buoy: 25 m at most.
To commercial fishing vessels: at least 300 m.
To their set gear: at least 148 m.
To the boundary of aquaculture sites: at least 200 m.
fichas.ojo: This is the national minimum for external waters. Minimum age, licence type, bag limits, closed seasons, no-fishing zones and internal waters are set by each autonomous community, and every marine reserve has its own rules. Check them before you go.

fichas.para: What Portuguese law says about spearfishing on the mainland.
fichas.resumen: Recreational fishing licence, breath-hold only, daylight only, no bait, buoy within 30 m and 15 kg a day at most. Protected areas and Harbour Masters add restrictions.
como_es: Breath-hold only (Decree-Law 246/2000 as amended by Decree-Law 101/2013, art. 9) and with a recreational fishing licence.
Allowed tools: speargun (not powered by explosive or artificially compressed gas), shellfish knife, gaff hook (puxeiro) and arrilhada. No bait or groundbait (Portaria 14/2014, arts. 3 and 5).
Banned: carrying a speargun and breathing equipment on board at the same time, and carrying a cocked gun out of the water or where spearfishing is banned (art. 3).
Buoy compulsory, 30 m away at most; 20 m between spearfishers unless agreed; vessels 50 m from the buoy (arts. 4, 6 and 7).
Banned between sunset and sunrise, and in navigation channels of river bars and mouths, port access channels and buoyed channels (arts. 7 and 8).
15 kg a day per person at most, not counting the largest fish (art. 12).
Species you may not take when spearfishing (Annex I) include groupers, spiny lobsters, European lobster and bluefin tuna.
According to the DGRM, spearfishing is banned in the Berlengas Nature Reserve and throughout the Arrábida Nature Park; other protected areas have no-go zones.
medidas: Buoy: no more than 30 m from the spearfisher; at least 8 litres.
Between spearfishers: 20 m.
Vessels: 50 m from the buoy.
Catch: 15 kg a day, not counting the largest fish.
fichas.ojo: These rules come from Portaria 14/2014, which applies to the mainland; the Azores and Madeira have regional rules. Harbour Masters can add restrictions by notice and the species list may change: check with the DGRM and the Harbour Master before you go.
